An engineer takes the log of a number for a decibel calculation. A shop owner works out a power for a compound growth check. You tap the keys to build the sum, use the function keys for sin, cos, tan, log, square root and powers, and press equals to see the answer. Everything runs in your browser, so there is nothing to install.
content.tip: Trigonometry here uses degrees, so sin(30) is 0.5, the same as a school calculator in degree mode. Use brackets to control the order, such as (2+3) x 4, instead of relying on memory. Tap Back to remove one character instead of clearing the whole sum.
content.limit: Trigonometry uses degrees, not radians. Factorial only works for whole numbers from 0 to 170. Very long sums may be hard to read on a small screen, and the tool does not save your history.
content.example: Typing sin(30) and pressing = gives 0.5.
faq: Does sin use degrees or radians?
Degrees. Sin(30) gives 0.5, the same as a school calculator set to degrees. There is no radian mode on this page.
How do I work out a square root?
Tap sqrt, type the number, close the bracket if one opened, then press =. For example, sqrt(16) gives 4, and sqrt(2) gives about 1.4142.
What does the x squared key do?
It raises the number before it to the power of 2. Typing 5 then the squared key gives 25, and typing 10 then the squared key gives 100.
Can I use brackets in a sum?
Yes. Tap the bracket keys to group parts of the sum. For example, (2+3) x 4 gives 20, while 2+3 x 4 gives 14.

short.en: Add, subtract, multiply and divide fractions.

tools.meta_description: Add, subtract, multiply and divide fractions, simplified, with the decimal value.
steps: Type the first fraction as a top number and a bottom number.
Choose add, subtract, multiply or divide in the 'Operation' list.
Type the second fraction the same way.
Press Calculate Fraction, or just wait, because the result updates as you type.
Read the simplified fraction and its decimal value under the button.

content.use: Fraction Calculator adds, subtracts, multiplies and divides fractions and simplifies the answer. A student checks homework on adding halves and thirds. A cook halves a recipe that uses fractions of a cup. A worker splits a length into equal parts for a job. A teacher makes quick fraction questions for a class test without working them out by hand. You type the two fractions, choose the operation, and the tool shows the simplified fraction and its decimal value, so you can check your own working in seconds.
content.tip: The answer is always simplified, so 2/4 shows as 1/2. A whole number answer shows as a whole number, such as 2, not 2/1. For a mixed number, divide the top by the bottom yourself; for example 5/2 is 2 and 1/2.
content.limit: Only whole numbers are accepted in the top and bottom boxes. The bottom number cannot be zero, and dividing by a fraction of zero is not allowed. The decimal is rounded to 4 places.
content.example: 1/2 plus 1/3 equals 5/6, which is about 0.8333.
faq: How do I add 1/2 and 1/3?
Type 1 over 2, choose add, type 1 over 3, then press Calculate Fraction. The answer is 5/6, about 0.8333.
Why is the answer simplified?
The tool divides the top and bottom by their largest shared factor. That gives the simplest form, such as 1/2 instead of 2/4.
Can the bottom number be zero?
No. A fraction with zero on the bottom has no value, so the tool asks for a different number before it can work out the answer.
What does the decimal value mean?
It is the fraction as a decimal number. For 5/6 it is about 0.8333, rounded to 4 decimal places, which is easier to use on a calculator or a measuring tape.

short.en: Count characters, words and reading time.

tools.meta_description: Count characters, words, sentences and reading time in your browser, live as you type.
steps: Type or paste your text in the box.
Read the live counts below the box: Characters, Characters (no spaces), Words, Sentences, Paragraphs and Reading time.
Edit the text in the box and the counts update with every keystroke.
Use the Characters count when a form, post or message limits the length.

content.use: Character Counter counts the characters in your text as you type, so you can check a limit before you submit or post. A student checks that an essay title fits the limit. A job applicant checks that a cover letter fits the box on the form. A writer checks that a post fits the character limit of a social site. A shop owner checks that a product name fits the label. The counts update live with every keystroke, so there is nothing to press. Words, sentences, paragraphs and reading time are shown too, so the page works as a quick word counter as well. The text never leaves your browser.
content.tip: Check the count before you submit a form, because a form may cut off extra characters without warning. If the count looks high, check for extra spaces or repeated paragraphs at the end of the text.
content.limit: The tool counts what you type; it does not check spelling, grammar or meaning. Reading time is a rough guide at 200 words per minute and is rounded up to whole minutes. A line break counts as one character, and most emoji count as two.
content.example: Pasting 'Hello world' shows Characters: 11, Characters (no spaces): 10, Words: 2 and Reading time: 1 min.
faq: Does a line break count as a character?

Yes. A line break is one character, and a space is one character too. If you press Enter twice, the two line breaks count as two characters, so a long text with many blank lines counts higher than it looks.
Does it count emoji as one character?

No. Most emoji count as two characters, because the browser stores them as two code units. A simple smiley counts as two, and a flag or a family emoji can count as more, so a post with many emoji may reach the limit sooner.
Can I count characters for a post?

Yes. Paste the post text in the box and read the Characters count. Compare it with the limit of the site you post on, and trim the text until the count fits. The count updates as you type, so you can watch it while you edit.
Why does the count change when I paste?

Pasting adds the characters of the pasted text to the count, including spaces and line breaks. If the count jumps more than you expect, the pasted text may have extra spaces or blank lines at the end, which you can delete.

short.en: Placeholder text for designs and layouts.

tools.meta_description: Generate lorem ipsum placeholder text in paragraphs, sentences or words, free in your browser.
steps: Choose Paragraphs, Sentences or Words in the 'Unit' list.
Choose how many you need in the 'Count' list.
Press Generate Lorem Ipsum.
Read the placeholder text in the box below the button.
Press Copy Text to copy it to the clipboard.

content.use: Lorem Ipsum Generator makes placeholder text for a design, so you can see how a page looks before the real words are ready. A designer fills a new website layout with paragraphs to check the spacing. A student makes a sample document to test a font. A developer fills a form with sentences to check that long text does not break the layout. You choose paragraphs, sentences or words, choose how many, and press the button to get the text. The words are the classic Latin filler text that designers have used for years, so readers focus on the layout, not the words. The text never leaves your browser.
content.tip: Use paragraphs for a page layout and sentences for a single block of text. The first sentence is always the classic 'Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet', so readers will know at once that the text is a placeholder.
content.limit: The text is placeholder Latin, not real English, so do not publish it as content. You can ask for 1 to 20 paragraphs, sentences or words at a time. The sentences come in the same order every time, so the output is the same for the same choices.
content.example: Choosing Sentences and 2 gives 'Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit. Sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.'
faq: What is lorem ipsum?
It is classic Latin placeholder text that designers have used for years to fill a layout. The words mean nothing in English, so readers focus on how the page looks instead of reading the words.
Can I use lorem ipsum in a real website?

No. It is only a placeholder for a design that is not finished yet. Replace it with real words before you publish, because visitors will not understand Latin filler text and may think the page is broken.
How many paragraphs should I use?
Use as many as the space needs. One paragraph fills a small block, three paragraphs fill a page section, and more than five is rare, because a real page would use real words by then.
Is the text the same every time?
Yes. The sentences come in the same order every time, so the same choices always give the same text. That makes it easy to compare two layouts, because only the layout changes, not the words.

short.en: Clean a list by dropping repeated lines.

tools.meta_description: Remove duplicate lines from a list, keeping the first copy of each line, free in your browser.
steps: Paste your lines in the box, one line per row.
Tick 'Case sensitive' if Apple and apple should count as different lines.
Press Remove Duplicates.
Read the cleaned list below the button and the count of removed lines.
Press Copy Result to copy the cleaned list.

content.use: Remove Duplicate Lines cleans a list by keeping the first copy of each line and dropping the rest, so a messy list becomes a clean one. A teacher removes repeated names from a class list. A shop owner removes repeated items from a stock list. A student removes repeated lines from notes copied from two sources. A worker cleans an email list before sending. You paste the lines, choose whether case matters, and press the button. Empty lines are removed too, and the order of the lines stays the same. The tool shows how many lines were removed, so you can check the result. The text never leaves your browser.
content.tip: Sort the list first if you want the kept lines in alphabetical order, because this tool keeps the order you pasted. Tick 'Case sensitive' only when Apple and apple really are different lines.
content.limit: Lines are trimmed, so extra spaces at the start or end do not stop a match. Empty lines are removed, and only the first copy of each line is kept. The tool does not sort the lines; use Sort Lines if you want them in order.
content.example: Pasting 'apple', 'banana', 'apple', 'cherry' and 'banana' on separate lines keeps apple, banana and cherry, and reports 2 duplicate lines removed.
faq: Does it keep the first or the last copy?
The first copy. The first time a line appears it is kept, and every later copy of the same line is removed. The order of the kept lines is the order they first appeared in your list.
Are blank lines removed?
Yes. Empty lines are removed from the result, so the cleaned list has no blank rows. If you need a blank line between groups, add it back yourself after you copy the cleaned list.
Is it case sensitive?
Only if you tick the box. With the box unticked, Apple and apple count as the same line, and only the first one is kept. With the box ticked, they count as different lines, and both are kept.
What happens to the order of the lines?

Nothing. The kept lines stay in the order you pasted them, because the tool only removes copies, it does not sort. If you want them in alphabetical order, open Sort Lines next and sort the cleaned list.

short.en: Sort lines A to Z, by number or length.

tools.meta_description: Sort lines of text A to Z, Z to A, by number or by length, free in your browser.
steps: Paste your lines in the box, one line per row.
Choose the order in the 'Sort order' list, such as A to Z or Numbers, smallest first.
Tick 'Ignore empty lines' to leave blank lines out of the result.
Press Sort Lines.
Read the sorted list below the button, or press Copy Result to copy it.

content.use: Sort Lines puts a list in order, so you can find things fast instead of reading the whole list. A teacher sorts student names from A to Z. A shop owner sorts product codes by number. A worker sorts a list of tasks from shortest to longest. A student sorts notes by the length of each line. You paste the lines, choose the order, and press the button. A to Z and Z to A use the alphabet, Numbers puts the smallest number first, and the length orders sort by how long each line is. The original text is not changed; the sorted list appears below the box. The text never leaves your browser.
content.tip: Use 'Numbers, smallest first' for lists that start with a number, such as '2 apples' and '10 apples'. Lines that do not start with a number go to the end of the list.
content.limit: Sorting is by the alphabet, so capital letters sort before small letters in some browsers. Lines that do not start with a number go to the end when you sort by number. The original text in the box is not changed.
content.example: Sorting 'banana', 'apple' and 'cherry' from A to Z gives apple, banana and cherry.
faq: How are numbers sorted?
By value, smallest first. A line that starts with 2 comes before a line that starts with 10, because 2 is smaller than 10. Lines that do not start with a number go to the end of the list.
What happens to empty lines?
It depends on the tick box. With 'Ignore empty lines' ticked, blank lines are left out of the result. With it unticked, blank lines stay in the list and sort to the top.
Does sorting change the original text?
No. The text in the box stays as you typed it, and the sorted list appears below the button. You can change the order and press the button again to sort the same lines differently.
Can I sort numbers and words together?
Yes, with the number order. Lines that start with a number sort by that number, and lines that start with a word go to the end, in alphabetical order among themselves.

short.en: Hear your text read aloud in the browser.

tools.meta_description: Hear text read aloud in your browser with your device voices, speed and pitch controls.
steps: Type or paste the text in the box.
Choose a voice in the 'Voice' list, if your browser offers more than one.
Move the Speed and Pitch sliders if you want it faster, slower, higher or lower.
Press Speak to hear the text read aloud.
Press Stop to end it early.

content.use: Text to Speech reads your text aloud in the browser, so you can listen instead of reading. A student listens to notes while walking. A writer hears how a sentence sounds before publishing it. A parent reads a story aloud with the device while cooking. A language learner hears the sound of English words. You type or paste the text, choose a voice if your browser offers more than one, set the speed and pitch, and press Speak. The voice comes from your device and browser, so the voices on offer differ from one device to another. The text never leaves your browser.
content.tip: Short sentences read more clearly than very long ones, so split a long paragraph before you press Speak. If a voice sounds wrong, try another voice from the list, because voices differ by device.
content.limit: Voices come from your device and browser, and some browsers offer no voice choice at all. Long text may be cut off by the browser, and the spoken audio cannot be downloaded from this page. The tool does not work in browsers without speech support.
content.example: Typing 'Hello, this is a test.' and pressing Speak reads the sentence aloud in the chosen voice.
faq: Which browsers can read text aloud?

Most modern browsers, including Chrome and Edge on desktop and Android, and Safari on iPhone and Mac. If the Speak button says your browser does not support it, try Chrome, which has the widest voice support.
Can I change the voice?

Yes, if your device offers more than one. The Voice list shows every voice your browser knows, and you can pick one before you press Speak. Some devices offer only one voice, and some offer none to choose.
Why is there no voice to choose?
Your device or browser has no extra voices installed. The tool then uses the default voice, and Speak still works. Installing a voice in your device settings may add more choices to the list.
Can I download the spoken audio?
No. The voice is made live by your browser and is not saved as a file. This page has no download for the audio, so if you need a recording, use a screen recorder or a voice recorder app.

short.en: Full Markdown preview: tables, task lists, footnotes.

tools.meta_description: Preview Markdown as formatted text in your browser, live as you type, with tables, task lists and footnotes.
steps: Type or paste Markdown in the box; the preview updates as you type.
Make a table with a header row, a row of dashes, then the rows, like | Item | Price |.
Make a task list with - [ ] for an open item and - [x] for a done item.
Add a footnote with [^1] in the text and [^1]: the note at the bottom.
Press Copy HTML to copy the formatted result, or Download HTML to save it as a page.

content.use: Markdown Previewer turns Markdown text into a formatted preview as you type, using the marked library for full CommonMark plus GitHub-style tables, task lists and footnotes. A writer checks a blog post with headings, bold words, tables and a footnote before publishing. A student drafts notes with a to-do list and a table of results. The preview shows the word count and reading time, and you can copy or download the formatted HTML.
content.tip: A table needs a header row and a row of dashes under it, or it stays as plain text. Write a footnote as [^1] where you want the number, then add [^1]: the note itself at the bottom of the document. If the preview looks empty, check that the text is in the box and not only in the preview pane.
content.limit: Raw HTML in your text is escaped and shown as text, never run, so no HTML tags, scripts or embedded pages are rendered. Diagrams, maths formulas and raw HTML blocks are not supported. Footnotes always render at the bottom of the preview.
content.example:
Typing '| Item | Price |
| --- | --- |
| Pen | 50 |' shows a real two-column table, and adding 'See the note[^1]' with '[^1]: Prices include tax.' at the bottom shows a numbered footnote link.
faq: Does the preview support tables?
Yes. Write a header row, a row of dashes, then the rows, like | Item | Price | on the first line, | --- | --- | on the second, and | Pen | 50 | on the third. The preview shows a real table.
How do I add a footnote?
Put [^1] in the text where you want the number, then add a line [^1]: your note at the bottom of the document. The preview shows a numbered link that jumps to the note.
What is a task list and how do I make one?
A task list is a list with checkboxes. Write - [ ] for an open item and - [x] for a done item, one per line. The preview shows real checkboxes you can tick.
Can I download the formatted preview as HTML?
Yes. Press Download HTML to save the preview as a page you can open in any browser, or Copy HTML to paste the formatted result into another app.

short.en: Styled Unicode text for names and posts.

tools.meta_description: Turn plain text into bold, italic, script and more Unicode styles, free in your browser.
steps: Type a word or short phrase in the box.
Read the styled versions below the box: Bold, Italic, Monospace, Script and more.
Press the Copy button next to a style to copy that version.
Paste the copied text where you want it, such as a profile name or a message.

content.use: Fancy Text Generator changes plain text into styled Unicode letters, so a name or message stands out. A student styles a profile name with bold letters. A shop owner styles a sale announcement with script letters. A writer styles a heading with monospace letters. A friend sends a message in circled letters for fun. You type the words once and the page shows them in eight styles, each with its own Copy button. The styles are special Unicode characters, not real formatting, so they work in most apps but may look different on some devices. The text never leaves your browser.
content.tip: Bold and italic work in most apps, but script and double-struck letters may show as boxes on old devices, so test the copied text where you plan to use it. Keep the text short, because styled letters take more space.
content.limit: Styled text is made of special Unicode characters, not real formatting, so some apps and old devices may show boxes instead of letters. Screen readers may read styled letters oddly, so do not use them for important information.
content.example: Typing 'Hello' shows Bold as '𝐇𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐨' and Script as 'ℋℯ𝓁𝓁𝓄'.
faq: Will the styled text work everywhere?

In most apps, yes. Bold, italic and monospace work almost everywhere, but script and double-struck letters may show as boxes on old devices. Test the copied text where you plan to use it before you publish.
Why do some styles look like boxes?

The device does not have a font with those Unicode letters. Each style uses special characters, and if the font has no drawing for a character, the device shows a box instead. Try another style, which may have better font support.
Can I use styled text on social media?

Yes. Most social apps accept Unicode letters in names, bios and posts, because they are ordinary text characters. Some apps may show them differently, so check how the name looks on another phone before you keep it.
Is the text still searchable?
Not always. A search looks for plain letters, and styled letters are different characters, so a search for Hello may not find a styled Hello. Use plain text for anything people need to search for.

short.en: Replace every match in your text at once.

tools.meta_description: Find and replace every match of a word or phrase in your text, free in your browser.
steps: Paste your text in the box.
Type the text to find in the 'Find' box.
Type the replacement in the 'Replace with' box, or leave it empty to delete the matches.
Tick 'Match case' if Cat and cat should be treated as different words.
Press Replace All, then read the new text and the count of replacements below the button.

content.use: Find and Replace changes every match of a word or phrase in your text at once, so you do not have to fix each one by hand. A writer changes a character name through a whole story. A student fixes a repeated spelling mistake in an essay. A shop owner changes a price word in a list of products. A worker updates a date in a long note. You paste the text, type what to find and what to put in its place, and press Replace All. The tool counts the replacements, so you can check that every match was changed. The new text appears below the button, ready to copy. The text never leaves your browser.
content.tip: Leave the 'Replace with' box empty to delete the matches. Check the replacement count after you press the button, because a count of 0 means the find text was not in the text at all.
content.limit: The search is plain text, not a pattern, so special characters are treated as ordinary letters. Replacing cannot be undone on this page, so copy the new text before you change the input. The tool replaces every match at once.
content.example: Replacing 'cat' with 'dog' in 'The cat sat on the cat mat' gives 'The dog sat on the dog mat', with 2 replacements.
faq: Does it replace every match?
Yes. Pressing Replace All changes every match in the text at once, and the status line tells you how many were replaced. If the count is 0, the find text was not in the text at all.
Is the search case sensitive?
Only if you tick the box. With the box unticked, Cat and cat count as the same word, and both are replaced. With the box ticked, only the exact capitalisation you typed is replaced.
Can I use special characters in the search?
Yes. The search is plain text, so a dot, a star or a bracket is treated as an ordinary letter, not as a pattern. That makes it safe to search for prices, file names and other text with symbols.
Does it change the original text?

No. The text in the box stays as you typed it, and the new text appears below the button. Copy the new text before you change the input, because pressing the button again works on the text in the box.

short.en: Flesch score and grade for your text.

tools.meta_description: Check readability with the Flesch Reading Ease score and grade level, free in your browser.
steps: Paste your text in the box.
Press Check Readability.
Read the Flesch Reading Ease score, the grade level, and the word, sentence and syllable counts.
Compare the score with the guide: 90 and above is Very easy, 60 to 70 is Standard, below 30 is Very difficult.

content.use: Readability Checker scores your text with the Flesch Reading Ease and the Flesch-Kincaid grade, so you can tell how easy it is to read. A writer checks that a blog post is easy for most readers. A teacher checks that a handout fits the class level. A student checks an essay before handing it in. A shop owner checks that a product note is plain and clear. You paste the text and press the button. The tool counts words, sentences and syllables, then works out the scores and a plain label, from Very easy to Very difficult. The scores describe the text, not the reader, and syllables are estimated by a rule. The text never leaves your browser.
content.tip: Short sentences and short words raise the score, so split long sentences if the text scores below 60. Compare two versions of the same text to see which one reads more easily.
content.limit: Syllables are estimated by a rule that counts vowel groups, not by a dictionary, so unusual words may score slightly differently. The score describes the text, not the reader, and a low score does not mean the text is wrong.
content.example: The two sentences 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog. Pack my box with five dozen liquor jugs.' score 93.7, grade 2.3, Very easy.
faq: What is a good readability score?

A Flesch Reading Ease of 60 to 70 is Standard, which most adults read with ease. Above 80 is Easy, and above 90 is Very easy. Below 30 is Very difficult, and it suits a specialist reader, not a general one.
How are syllables counted?

By a rule, not by a dictionary. The tool counts groups of vowels in each word, takes one away for a silent e at the end, and counts at least one syllable per word. Unusual words may score slightly differently.
What is the Flesch Reading Ease score?

It is a score from 0 to 100 that rates how easy a text is to read, from the average sentence length and the average syllables per word. A higher score means easier reading, and a lower score means harder reading.
Does it work for other languages?
Not really. The Flesch formulas were made for English, and the syllable rule counts English vowel groups. Text in another language may give a score, but the score will not mean the same thing.

short.en: See which words you use most.

tools.meta_description: Count how often each word appears in your text, most used first, free in your browser.
steps: Paste your text in the box.
Tick 'Ignore common words' to leave out words such as the and and.
Choose how many words to show in the 'Show' list.
Press Count Word Frequency.
Read the list below the button: the most used word first, with its count.

content.use: Word Frequency counts how often each word appears in your text, so you can see what a piece of writing is really about. A student checks whether an essay repeats one word too much. A writer checks the key words in an article before choosing a title. A teacher checks the common words in a reading passage. A shop owner checks which words customers use most in reviews. You paste the text, choose whether to ignore common words such as the and and, and press the button. The list shows the most used word first, with its count, and words with the same count are listed in alphabetical order. The text never leaves your browser.
content.tip: Tick 'Ignore common words' to see the real key words, because the and and are the most used words in almost every text. A word that appears far more than the rest is usually the topic of the text.
content.limit: Only words made of English letters are counted; numbers, punctuation and words in other scripts are ignored. Words are counted without capitals, so Cat and cat count as the same word.
content.example: In 'the cat and the dog and the bird' with common words ignored, bird, cat and dog each show 1.
faq: What counts as a word?

A run of English letters. Numbers, punctuation and spaces break words apart, and words are counted without capitals, so Cat and cat count as the same word. Words in other scripts are ignored by this tool.
Why are common words left out?

Only when you tick the box. Common words such as the and and appear in almost every text, so they hide the real key words. Unticking the box shows every word, including the common ones, with their counts.
Can I see all the words, not just the top ones?
Yes. Choose All words in the Show list, and the tool lists every different word in the text, most used first. For a long text the list is long, so Top 10 or Top 20 is easier to read.
Does it count words in other languages?
No. This tool only counts words made of English letters, so Urdu, Arabic and other scripts are ignored. If your text is in another language, use Word Counter, which counts words by spaces instead.

short.en: Turn your spoken words into written text.

tools.meta_description: Dictate and turn your speech into text in your browser, free with no sign-up.
steps: Choose your language in the 'Language' list.
Press Start Listening and allow the microphone when your browser asks.
Speak clearly into the microphone and watch the words appear in the transcript box.
Press Stop when you finish speaking.
Press Copy Transcript to copy the text for use anywhere.

content.use: Speech to Text turns your spoken words into written text, so you can write without typing. A student dictates notes while walking. A writer speaks a first draft and edits it later. A shop owner dictates a product note while packing an order. A person with a sore wrist writes messages by voice. You choose your language, press Start Listening, allow the microphone when your browser asks, and speak clearly. The words appear in the transcript box as you speak, and you can copy the text when you stop. The transcript is built in your browser from the speech service of your browser, and the text stays with you.
content.tip: Speak in a quiet room and hold the microphone near your mouth, because background noise and a far microphone cause wrong words. Short sentences work better than long ones, and a pause between sentences helps the tool tell where one sentence ends.
content.limit: The tool needs a browser that supports speech recognition, such as Chrome on desktop or Android, and it needs a microphone. Your browser may send the audio to its own speech service to turn it into text, so do not dictate private or secret words. Recognition is not perfect, so check the transcript and fix wrong words before you use it.
content.example: Speaking 'Hello, this is a test' with English (US) chosen shows the same words in the transcript box.
faq: Which browsers can listen?

Chrome on desktop and Android supports speech recognition. Other browsers may not offer it, and the tool then shows a message that your browser does not support listening. If you see that message, try Chrome or Edge on desktop or Android.
Does my voice leave my browser?

It may. Your browser can send the audio to its own speech service to turn it into words, and that service is run by the browser maker, not by this site. Do not dictate passwords, private names or secret words.
Why are some words wrong?

Speech recognition guesses words from sound, so similar sounding words can be mixed up, and background noise makes it worse. Speak slowly in a quiet room, and read the transcript at the end to fix any wrong words.
Can I dictate in Urdu?

Yes, if your browser offers Urdu in the Language list. Choose Urdu before you press Start Listening, then speak in Urdu. If Urdu is missing from the list, your browser does not offer it on this device.

short.en: Turn a title into a clean URL slug.

tools.meta_description: Turn any title into a clean URL slug with lowercase letters and hyphens, free in your browser.
steps: Type or paste your title in the box.
Read the slug below the box: it updates live with every keystroke.
Press Copy Slug to copy it.
Paste the slug at the end of your page address.

content.use: Slug Generator turns a page title into a clean slug for the address of the page, so links stay short and easy to read. A blogger turns a post title into a link that readers can remember. A shop owner turns a product name into a neat address for the product page. A teacher turns a lesson title into a link for students. You type the title once, and the tool makes it lowercase, changes spaces to hyphens, removes accents and special signs, and trims hyphens from the ends. The slug updates live as you type, and the text never leaves your browser.
content.tip: Keep titles short before you make a slug, because a long title makes a long link that is hard to share. Remove words such as 'the' and 'and' from the title if the slug still looks long.
content.limit: The slug uses English letters, numbers and hyphens only, so words in other scripts are removed. Very long titles are not cut short, so check the length before you use the slug. A slug is only the last part of an address, not a full link.
content.example: Typing 'Hello World! My First Post' gives the slug 'hello-world-my-first-post'.
faq: What is a slug?
The last part of a page address, made of lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens. A post titled 'Hello World' can live at an address that ends with hello-world, which is easy to read and share.
Why are spaces changed to hyphens?
Spaces are not allowed in an address, so they are changed to hyphens. A hyphen is read as a word break by search engines, while an underscore is not, so hyphens are the safer choice.
What happens to accents?
Accents are removed and the plain letter is kept, so 'café' becomes 'cafe'. This keeps the slug to plain English letters, which every browser and server can handle.
Can I use a slug with numbers?
Yes. Numbers are kept as they are, so 'Top 10 Tips' becomes 'top-10-tips'. Only letters, numbers and hyphens appear in the slug.

short.en: Convert JSON data into YAML format.

tools.meta_description: Convert JSON into clean YAML in your browser, free with no sign-up.
steps: Paste your JSON in the box.
Press Convert to YAML.
Read the YAML below the button.
Press Copy Result to copy the YAML.

content.use: JSON to YAML changes data from JSON form into YAML form, so you can use it where YAML is needed. A developer moves settings from a JSON file into a YAML config file. A student turns a JSON sample from class into YAML for a project. A writer prepares data for a site that reads YAML files. You paste the JSON, press Convert to YAML, and the tool shows the same data with YAML indents instead of braces and commas. Lists and nested data are kept in order, and the data never leaves your browser.
content.tip: Check that your JSON is valid before you convert, because one missing comma or bracket stops the tool. JSON Formatter on this site can format and check the JSON first.
content.limit: The tool reads standard JSON only, so comments and trailing commas are not allowed. Very large files may be slow, and the YAML output uses the js-yaml library in your browser. Dates and other special values are treated as plain text or numbers.
content.example: Pasting {"name": "Ali", "age": 30} gives YAML with 'name: Ali' on the first line and 'age: 30' on the second.
faq: Is my JSON kept private?
Yes. The conversion runs in your browser, and the JSON is not sent to a server. The YAML library loads from a public CDN, but your data stays on your device.
Why does the tool reject my JSON?
The most common cause is a missing comma, an extra comma at the end, or quotes that do not match. Paste the JSON into JSON Formatter first, which points out the mistake.
Does it keep the order of my data?
Yes. Keys stay in the order they appear in the JSON, and lists stay in order too. Nested objects are shown with deeper indents.
What is YAML used for?
YAML is a plain text format for settings and config files, used by many tools and services. It uses indents instead of braces, so it is easy to read and edit by hand.

short.en: Convert YAML data into JSON format.

tools.meta_description: Convert YAML into JSON in your browser, free with no sign-up.
steps: Paste your YAML in the box.
Press Convert to JSON.
Read the JSON below the button, shown with two-space indents.
Press Copy Result to copy the JSON.

content.use: YAML to JSON changes data from YAML form into JSON form, so you can use it where JSON is needed. A developer reads a YAML config file and turns it into JSON for an app. A student turns a YAML sample from a tutorial into JSON for a class task. A tester prepares JSON data from a YAML file. You paste the YAML, press Convert to JSON, and the tool shows the same data with braces and commas, using two-space indents. Lists and nested data are kept in order, and the data never leaves your browser.
content.tip: YAML cares about indents, so check that each level uses the same number of spaces. Mixed tabs and spaces are the most common cause of a YAML error.
content.limit: The tool reads standard YAML only, and it does not run YAML tags or custom types. Very large files may be slow, and the YAML output uses the js-yaml library in your browser. A YAML file with tabs for indents may fail, so use spaces.
content.example: Pasting 'name: Ali' on one line and 'age: 30' on the next gives JSON with "name": "Ali" and "age": 30.
faq: Is my YAML kept private?
Yes. The conversion runs in your browser, and the YAML is not sent to a server. The YAML library loads from a public CDN, but your data stays on your device.
Why does the tool reject my YAML?
The most common cause is mixed tabs and spaces, or a wrong indent. YAML needs the same spaces at each level, so check the indents and try again.
Does it keep my lists in order?
Yes. Keys stay in the order they appear in the YAML, and lists stay in order too. Nested data is shown with deeper indents in the JSON.
Can it read more than one document?
No. The tool reads a single YAML document. If your file has more than one document split by three dashes, convert each one on its own.

short.en: Convert JSON data into XML format.

tools.meta_description: Convert JSON into XML in your browser, free with no sign-up.
steps: Paste your JSON in the box.
Press Convert to XML.
Read the XML below the button, inside a root tag.
Press Copy Result to copy the XML.

content.use: JSON to XML changes data from JSON form into XML form, so you can use it where XML is needed. A developer sends JSON data to an old system that only reads XML. A student turns a JSON sample into XML for a class task. A tester prepares XML data from a JSON file. You paste the JSON, press Convert to XML, and the tool shows the same data with tags, inside one root tag. Lists become repeated tags, and the data never leaves your browser.
content.tip: Give lists a clear name in the JSON, because each item becomes a tag with that name. A list called 'items' becomes repeated 'item' tags, which is easy to read.
content.limit: Keys must be valid tag names, so keys with spaces or strange signs are changed to safe names. Numbers and true or false values are shown as text, and the root tag is always called 'root'. Very large files may be slow.
content.example: Pasting {"name": "Ali"} gives the XML <root><name>Ali</name></root>.
faq: Does my JSON stay private?
Yes. The conversion runs in your browser, and the JSON is not sent to a server. Your data stays on your device.
What is the root tag?
Every XML file needs one top tag, so the tool wraps all the data in a tag called 'root'. If you need a different top name, change the word 'root' in the copied XML.
How are lists shown?
Each item in a list becomes its own tag. A list of two names becomes two 'item' tags inside the list tag, in the same order as the JSON.
What happens to numbers?
Numbers are shown as text inside tags, because XML has no number type. When you read the XML back, turn the text into numbers again.

short.en: Convert XML data into JSON format.

tools.meta_description: Convert XML into JSON in your browser, free with no sign-up.
steps: Paste your XML in the box.
Press Convert to JSON.
Read the JSON below the button, shown with two-space indents.
Press Copy Result to copy the JSON.

content.use: XML to JSON changes data from XML form into JSON form, so you can use it where JSON is needed. A developer reads an XML reply from an old system and turns it into JSON for an app. A student turns an XML sample into JSON for a class task. A tester prepares JSON data from an XML file. You paste the XML, press Convert to JSON, and the tool shows the same data with braces and commas. Tags become keys, repeated tags become lists, and the data never leaves your browser.
content.tip: Check that every opening tag has a matching closing tag, because one missing tag stops the tool. A single top tag must wrap all the data, which is how XML works.
content.limit: The tool reads the tags and text of the XML, but it does not keep comments or processing notes. Tag details such as attributes are shown with an @ sign before the name. Very large files may be slow.
content.example: Pasting <root><name>Ali</name></root> gives JSON with "root" holding "name": "Ali".
faq: Is my XML kept private?
Yes. The conversion runs in your browser, and the XML is not sent to a server. Your data stays on your device.
Why does the tool reject my XML?
The most common cause is a tag that is not closed, or more than one top tag. XML needs one top tag and every tag closed in order, so check the tags and try again.
How are repeated tags shown?
Repeated tags with the same name become a list in the JSON. Two 'item' tags become one list with two values, in the same order as the XML.
What happens to tag attributes?
An attribute is shown as a key with an @ sign before its name, next to the text of the tag. The text itself is shown under the key '#text' when a tag has both.

short.en: Convert a JSON list into a CSV table.

tools.meta_description: Convert a JSON list into a CSV table in your browser, free with no sign-up.
steps: Paste your JSON list in the box.
Press Convert to CSV.
Read the table below the button, with one row per item.
Press Copy Result to copy the CSV, or Download CSV to save it.

content.use: JSON to CSV changes a JSON list into a table, so you can open it in a spreadsheet. A developer turns app data into a CSV file for a report. A shop owner turns an order list into a table for Excel. A student turns a JSON sample into a table for class. You paste the JSON list, press Convert to CSV, and the tool shows the first row as column names and one row per item. Nested data is flattened with dots between the names, and the data never leaves your browser.
content.tip: Make sure every item in the list has the same fields, because a missing field leaves an empty cell in that row. If a value holds a comma, the tool wraps it in quotes so the table stays correct.
content.limit: The tool needs a JSON list of items, so a single object on its own will not work. Nested objects are flattened with dots, and lists inside an item are kept as JSON text. Very large lists may be slow.
content.example: Pasting [{"name": "Ali", "age": 30}, {"name": "Sara", "age": 25}] gives a table with 'name,age' on the first row, then 'Ali,30' and 'Sara,25'.
faq: Does the tool send my JSON anywhere?
No. The conversion runs in your browser, and the JSON is not sent to a server. Your data stays on your device.
Why does the tool ask for a list?
A CSV table needs rows, and each item in the JSON list becomes one row. A single object has no rows, so wrap it in square brackets to make a list of one item.
How are nested values shown?
A value inside another object is flattened with a dot, so an address with a city becomes a column called 'address.city'. A list inside an item is kept as JSON text in one cell.
Can I open the result in Excel?
Yes. Copy the table or download it as a .csv file, then open it in Excel or Google Sheets. Values with commas are wrapped in quotes, so the columns stay in place.

short.en: Decode a JWT and verify its HMAC signature.

tools.meta_description: Decode a JWT token to read its header and payload, and verify HS256, HS384 and HS512 signatures with a pasted secret, free in your browser.
steps: Paste your JWT token in the box.
Press Decode Token.
Read the header and payload below the button, shown as formatted JSON, with the expiry time explained in plain words.
To check the signature, paste the secret in the secret box and press Verify Signature. The result says VERIFIED, INVALID, or cannot verify.

content.use: JWT Decoder reads a JSON Web Token and shows the header and payload inside it, so you can check what a token holds, and it can also verify the signature for HMAC tokens. A developer checks the user id and roles in a login token, then pastes the secret to confirm the token is real and not edited. A student learns how a JWT is built. Verification uses the WebCrypto API in your browser, and your secret never leaves your device.
content.tip: Verification only works for HMAC tokens (HS256, HS384, HS512) when you paste the exact secret that signed the token. The sample token from jwt.io verifies with the secret 'your-256-bit-secret'. If the token uses RS256 or ES256, the tool says it cannot verify, because those need a public key, not a secret.
content.limit: The tool only verifies HMAC signatures with a secret you paste. RS256 and ES256 tokens cannot be verified here, because they need a public key. A token with alg 'none' has no signature at all, so it is never shown as verified and always carries a warning. Your secret is used only in your browser and is never sent anywhere.
content.example: Decoding the sample token from jwt.io shows the header {"alg": "HS256", "typ": "JWT"} and the payload with the name John Doe. Pasting the secret 'your-256-bit-secret' and pressing Verify Signature shows VERIFIED. Pasting a wrong secret shows INVALID.
faq: How do I verify a token's signature?

Paste the token, press Decode Token, then paste the secret that signed the token in the secret box and press Verify Signature. The tool shows VERIFIED if the signature matches, or INVALID if it does not.
Why does my token say cannot verify?
The tool can only verify HMAC tokens (HS256, HS384, HS512) with a pasted secret. RS256 and ES256 tokens need a public key, so the tool says it cannot verify them instead of guessing.
What does alg none mean?
Alg 'none' means the token has no signature at all, so anyone could have written it. The tool shows a clear warning and never marks such a token as verified.
Is my secret sent anywhere?
No. Your secret is used only in your browser by the WebCrypto API to check the signature, and it is never sent to any server. Closing the page clears it.

short.en: Make MD5 and SHA hashes of text or a file.

tools.meta_description: Generate MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 hashes of text or a file, free in your browser.
steps: Type or paste your text in the box, or choose a file with the file button.
Choose MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512 in the 'Algorithm' list.
Press Generate Hash.
Press Copy Hash to copy the result.

content.use: Hash Generator makes a fingerprint of text or a file, so you can check that it has not changed. A developer checks that a downloaded file matches the hash on the download page. A student makes a SHA-256 hash of a password for a class task. A tester checks that a file sent by email arrived whole. You type text or choose a file, pick MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512, and press Generate Hash. The hash is made in your browser, and the text or file never leaves your device.
content.tip: Use SHA-256 when you check a download, because MD5 and SHA-1 are old and can be faked. Compare the whole hash, not just the first few signs, because two different files can share the start.
content.limit: SHA hashes need a secure page, and they run in the browser with the built-in crypto tools. MD5 and SHA-1 are shown for old checks only and should not be used for new security. A hash cannot be turned back into the text, so keep the original.
content.example: Hashing the word 'hello' with SHA-256 gives 2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824, and with MD5 it gives 5d41402abc4b2a76b9719d911017c592.
faq: Is my text or file kept private?
Yes. The hash is made in your browser, and the text or file is not sent to a server. The MD5 library loads from a public CDN, but your data stays on your device.
Which hash should I use?
Use SHA-256 for most checks, because it is fast and safe. MD5 and SHA-1 are old and can be faked, so use them only when an old system asks for them.
Can I get the text back from a hash?
No. A hash is one way, so the text cannot be rebuilt from it. If you lose the text, the hash alone will not bring it back.
Why does the same text give the same hash?
A hash is made only from the input, so the same text always gives the same hash. One changed letter gives a very different hash, which is how a hash shows a change.

short.en: Encode and decode URLs and text safely.

tools.meta_description: Encode and decode URLs and text with percent encoding in your browser, free with no sign-up.
steps: Type or paste your URL or text in the box.
Choose 'Encode a value' for a word or name, or 'Encode a full URL' to keep the address working.
Press Encode to encode it, or Decode to decode it.
Press Copy Result to copy the result.

content.use: URL Encode Decode changes text so it is safe to put in a web address, and changes it back again. A developer encodes a search word with a space before adding it to a link. A student encodes a file name with brackets for a shared link. A tester decodes a long address to read what it holds. You paste the text, press Encode to change spaces and signs into percent codes, or press Decode to change the codes back. The text never leaves your browser.
content.tip: Encode only the part that needs it, such as a search word, and leave the rest of the address alone. If the whole address is encoded, the slashes and colons are encoded too, and the link will not work.
content.limit: The tool encodes text with the standard percent rules, so a few signs such as letters, numbers, hyphens and dots are left as they are. Decoding text that was never encoded may fail, and the tool then shows a message.
content.example: Encoding 'hello world' gives 'hello%20world', and decoding 'hello%20world' gives 'hello world' back.
faq: Why encode a URL?
An address cannot hold spaces or many signs, so they are changed into percent codes. A space becomes %20, and the link then works in every browser.
What does 'Encode a full URL' do?

It encodes spaces and odd signs but keeps the slashes, colons and question marks that make the address work. Use it when a link has a space in it. To put an address inside another address, choose 'Encode a value' instead, which encodes every sign.
Can I decode any address?
Yes, if it was encoded with the same rules. If the text has a lone percent sign or a bad code, the tool shows a message instead of a wrong result.
Is my text kept private?
Yes. The encoding runs in your browser, and the text is not sent to a server. Your text stays on your device.
